messages.subject: Re: Legend Label Issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Sat, Nov 20, 2010 at 8:18 AM, Dmitry Berman <rave...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dennis,
>
> Thanks that got it, and yes "section" is a better label. But, why did it get it? I'm not sure of what I just did to there, be totally honest....
>
> Dmitry
>

When you use the manual scale, it is expected that you want to change more than the legend title - typically, one either wants to change the group labels, colors, shapes, linetypes, etc. I've just kind of learned through experience that if all you want to do is change the legend title, it's easiest to avoid manual scales. There are others who can probably explain the technical reasons better than I.

Even better would have been to plan ahead. Knowing that you wanted different linetypes for different sections, you could have melted the data to create a factor variable whose levels are the variable names Verbal and Math and whose values are stacked in the constructed variable 'value'. This little trick was one of the reasons the function was developed in the first place. Now you can map the variable names to linetype, have the names you want in the legend labels and the title you want by resetting the variable names in the melted data frame passed in the ggplot() call. Observe:

library(reshape2)
dm <- melt(d, id = 'Year')
names(dm) <- c('Year', 'Section', 'Score')
g <- ggplot(dm, aes(x = Year, y= Score))
g + geom_line(aes(linetype = Section)) + ...

No scale adjustment is necessary now and no need to rename the x and y labels (although you may want to still play with the axis ticks).

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: error with facet wrap and stat_bin2d
messages.subject_clean: error with facet wrap and stat_bin2d
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

The issue has to do with strings (I provide an example at the end).
The typical way to create your base in ggplot is with aes(), but there
is also the aes_string() function which can handle strings, so you do
not see any issue there.  However, aes_string() is just a special
parser to deal with text, so when you pass 'string2' to facet_wrap(),
in essence it cannot find the object.  There is an error when trying
to assign dimensions, because the "object" (i.e., string2) is empty.
Unquoting it will fix the problem.  I would also generally recommend
using aes() in ggplot(), but you may have a good reason for using
aes_string(), which is fine.  You will still need to unquote string2
in your call to facet_wrap().  If you need to pass it as text somehow,
I think you will need to create your own intermediate parser that
converts your text to a formula and then passes that formula to
facet_wrap().

Cheers,

Josh

#### Example data ####
## side note, using dput() on your data is a nice way
## to provide it via email that is easy for both parties to use
set.seed(810)
dat <- data.frame(float0 = abs(rnorm(150, 20, sd = 12)),
                  float1 = abs(rnorm(150, 90, 35)),
                  string2 = LETTERS[sample(1:7, 150, TRUE)])
summary(dat) # I tried to make it close to your summary

#### Plots ####
d <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = float1, y = float0, group = string2))
d + stat_bin2d() + geom_bin2d() # works
## Facetted without quotes works
d + stat_bin2d() + geom_bin2d() + facet_wrap(~ string2)

## just to show you can use it with aes_string()
d2 <- ggplot(dat, aes_string(x = 'float1', y = 'float0', group = 'string2'))
d2 + stat_bin2d() + geom_bin2d() + facet_wrap(~ string2)

Hi,

It's probably easiest with the tikzDevice device, where you could
encode LaTeX syntax in your axis labels. Something like,

library(ggplot2)
library(tikzDevice)

p = qplot(1:9, 1:9 * 1e3) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks= seq(1,9)*1e3, labels =
paste("\\textbf{",seq(1,9),"}000", sep=""))

tikz("test.tex", standAlone=TRUE)
print(p)
dev.off()

HTH,

baptiste

considered this myself, but it is not as easy as it might seem.
Firstly, there is the non-trivial time required to do it.  Secondly,
ggplot2 is somewhat unique, I think, in that virtually none of the
functions operate in isolation.  This makes documenting them in
isolation difficult.  To make an analogy, how would you describe what
a noun is and how to use a noun properly?  A verb? A direct object?

store" is an incorrect sentence, so to certain functions are properly

definitions out argument by argument.  I am personally of the opinion

messages.body_plain:
Hmm, well here is *a* way to pass a string to facet_wrap().  I have
never used python or PyR2 personally, so I don't know if this will
work in that context (using the same data as before):

d2 <- ggplot(dat, aes_string(x = 'float1', y = 'float0', group = 'string2'))
d2 + stat_bin2d() + geom_bin2d() +

  facet_wrap(substitute(~x, list(x=as.name <http://as.name>("string2"))))

As you can see, string2 is quoted, but now that is wrapped up in a
list whose value is substituted for x, so that what is finally passed
to facet_wrap() is ~string2.

HTH,

Josh

P.S. You are quite welcome; it is my pleasure to answer questions when I can.

I'm trying to use ggplot2 to draw a heat map. The code is as follows:

df <- data.frame(x=sample(LETTERS[1:10], 100, replace =T), y
=sample(LETTERS[1:10], 100, replace =T), z=runif(100, 1,
10))           # generate data sample

group=x), geom='tile')  # draw with default settings
p + scale_fill_gradient(low='white', high='steelblue',
formatter='percent')  # change color and format

The problem is that there are 2 legends. The top one is wanted with
correct color and format. How to remove the bottom one?

Thanks.

Hi:

Stefan is right as far as it goes, but it doesn't really get to Martin's labeling problem. Consider the following, using qplot() (the same happens in ggplot() ):

# (1)
qplot(x, y, data = df, stat = 'sum', group = x, fill = ..prop.., geom = 'tile')
# Replicate Stefan's suggestion: [Plot 1 in attachment]
qplot(x, y, data = df, stat = 'sum', group = x, fill = ..prop.., geom = 'tile') +
     scale_fill_gradient(low='white', high='steelblue')

# (2)
# Try to change the title on the legend:  [Plot 2 in attachment]
qplot(x, y, data = df, stat = 'sum', group = x, fill = ..prop.., geom = 'tile') +
     scale_fill_gradient('Percent')
# Add title change to Stefan's suggestion: [Plot 3 in attachment]
qplot(x, y, data = df, stat = 'sum', group = x, fill = ..prop.., geom = 'tile') +

     scale_fill_gradient('Percent', low='white', high='steelblue')

I don't think that should happen. Of course, if the simple title change doesn't work, then neither does the formatter = 'percent' argument, which seemed pretty reasonable to me and which doesn't appear to be the immediate source of the problem. I also tried [Plot 4 in attachment]

qplot(x, y, data = df, stat = 'sum', group = x, fill = ..prop.., geom = 'tile') +

    scale_fill_gradient(low='white', high='steelblue',

            breaks = seq(0.1, 0.5, by = 0.1),
            labels = c('10%', '20%', '30%', '40%', '50%'))

which puts the same title and breaks as the original legend, but it still prints two. It seems to me, at least on the surface, this has something to do with stat_sum() or the interaction of stat_sum() with geom_tile() [more likely].

Martin's code looks like a variation of the last example in the on-line help page of scale_gradient() except that he used stat_sum() to generate the constructed variable ..prop..  instead of using one of the geoms. It's entirely possible I'm not thinking outside the box enough to see the solution, though, and if so, I'd be happy to be edified.

messages.subject: Re: How to remove duplicated legends
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

ggplot2 tries to present as concise of legends as possible, however, when information is unique, there must be unique legends.  Two scales are involved here, scale_fill_gradient() and scale_size().  When the title of scale_fill_gradient() is changed, the title must also be changed on scale_size() in order for the legends to be collapsed.  There is a second issue, the formatting of the scale_fill_gradient() legend was changed, so it must also be changed on scale_size() in order for them to be collapsed.  However, scale_size() lacks a formatter argument.  Here is what the code would need to look like:

ggplot(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  stat_sum(aes(fill = ..prop.., group = x), geom = 'tile') +
  scale_fill_gradient('Percent', low='white', high='steelblue', formatter = 'percent') +
  scale_size('Percent', formatter = 'percent')

and here is a patch to scale_size() to make the above code actually work.

Cheers,

Josh

@Hadley, all I did was add a formatter = identity argument to the function and formatter = formatter to the super$new call.

ScaleSizeContinuous <- proto(ScaleContinuous, expr={
  doc <- TRUE
  common <- NULL
  .input <- .output <- "size"
  aliases <- c("scale_area", "scale_size")

  new <- function(., name=NULL, limits=NULL, breaks=NULL, labels=NULL, formatter = identity, trans = NULL, to = c(1, 6), legend = TRUE) {

    b_and_l <- check_breaks_and_labels(breaks, labels)

    .super$new(., name=name, limits=limits, breaks=b_and_l$breaks, labels=b_and_l$labels, formatter = formatter, trans=trans, variable = "size", to = to, legend = legend)
  }

  map <- function(., values) {
    rescale(values, .$to, .$input_set())
  }
  output_breaks <- function(.) .$map(.$input_breaks())

  objname <- "size_continuous"
  desc <- "Size scale for continuous variable"
  seealso <- list(
    "scale_manual" = "for sizing discrete variables"
  )
  desc_params <- list(
    "to" = "a numeric vector of length 2 that specifies the minimum and maximum size of the plotting symbol after transformation."
  )

  icon <- function(.) {
    pos <- c(0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75)
    circleGrob(pos, pos, r=(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4)/2.5), gp=gpar(fill="grey50", col=NA))
  }

  examples <- function(.) {
    (p <- qplot(mpg, cyl, data=mtcars, size=cyl))
    p + scale_size("cylinders")
    p + scale_size("number\nof\ncylinders")

    p + scale_size(to = c(0, 10))
    p + scale_size(to = c(1, 2))

    # Map area, instead of width/radius
    # Perceptually, this is a little better
    p + scale_area()
    p + scale_area(to = c(1, 25))

    # Also works with factors, but not a terribly good
    # idea, unless your factor is ordered, as in this example
    qplot(mpg, cyl, data=mtcars, size=factor(cyl))

    # To control the size mapping for discrete variable, use
    # scale_size_manual:
    last_plot() + scale_size_manual(values=c(2,4,6))

  }

})

messages.subject_clean: Multiple data sets and a faceting question
messages.body_plain:
I am using the ggplot2 package quite heavily for implementing
sensible plot methods for some process data objects I am working
on. I have encountered a few issues, which I can't solve or figure
out. I would highly appreciate any suggestions.

a) The key thing is that the process objects hold point process
data as well as discretely sampled continuous process data, and
I am producing the plot basically by superimposing the points
in a suitable way on top of the plot of the continuous process
in a way similar to the following example:

cData <- data.frame(time = seq(0,1,length.out = 100),
                    value = rnorm(100),
                    variable = "Cont. Process")

pointValue <- min(cData$value)-0.5

pData <- data.frame(time = cumsum(rexp(8,10)),
                    value = pointValue,
                    variable = "Point Process")

p <- ggplot(cData, aes(x = time, y = value, colour = variable)) +
      geom_line() +
       scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-2,-1,0,1,2,pointValue),
                          labels =  c("-2","-1","0","1","2",
                                      "Point Process"))

p + geom_point(data = pData)

I have two questions.

a.1) On the legend both geom's appear for both variables. Is there
any way to get only the geom on the legend that is plotted for the
variable.

a.2) Because the different data sets need to be plotted using
different
geoms due to their nature, one of them is "hidden" together with
possible
aesthetics in the geom_point call. In certain cases I find it useful
to
provide different default aesthetics for the points than the global
definition,
but the end user might find that another choice is more appropriate.
My functions return a ggplot object, and I know how a user can easily
override the global aesthetics, but is there any way a user can
override
the aesthetics specified for a particular geom?

b) Another issue is whether there is a mistake in the labels on the
faceted plot in the following example:

exData <- data.frame(time = rep(1:5,4),
                     id = factor(rep(c(1,2), each = 10)),
                     variable = factor(rep(c("a","b","a","b"), each =
5)),
                     value = rep(c(-2,-1,1,2), each = 5))

ggplot(exData, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
    facet_grid(id+variable~.)

I get labels (1,1), (2,2), (b,a), (b,a) and it should be
(1,a), (1,b), (2,a), (2,b). There is a similar behaviour
using facet_grid(.~id+variable)

Best regards, Niels

On Mon, Nov 22, 2010 at 8:46 PM, Feng Zhang <fzha...@gmail.com> wrote:

lol, is my code normally that bad? ;)

> Thanks.
>
> However I'm still confused how you managed to do this. As far as I can tell,

Redundant information in legends is collapsed.  ggplot calls many
scales with standard sets of default names, but when you change the
title of one scale (in this case: scale_fill_gradient("Percent")), the
legends are no longer redundant---they have different titles.
Further, you changed the legend labels by using the formatter argument
which means if you want a single legend, you must change all of the
scales to the same format also.

> you overwrite scale_size(). But in my original code, I didn't call

I do not overwrite scale_size (well, my patch gets added to the global
environment which is higher on the search path and pre-empts the
default, but those details aren't important), I just adjust the call
to scale_size() with custom arguments (i.e., the title to match the
scale_fill_gradient() and the formatter)

> scale_size(), at least not explicitly.

It is true, you did not explicitly, it was part of the
behind-the-scenes of ggplot2.  The sensible defaults are often fine,
but once you start customizing, you have to go all the way to each and
every scale (or you get the essentially redundant though technically
different legends you saw).  If you really want to learn more (and
have not already), I highly recommend reading the ggplot2 book.  It is
well written and it covers some of the structure/theory behind ggplot2
which will help make this sort of thing make sense.  If you already
have the book, trundle off to page 110 (section 6.5) paying special
note to the final paragraph of page 111.

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: error with geom_bar
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I just started to explore ggplot2 which seems like an awesome package.
However, I faced an error below

"stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to
adjust this.
Error in pmin(y, 0) : object 'y' not found"

My code is below:

p<-ggplot(Data,aes(x=DATE,y=PRINCIPAL))
p+geom_bar()

Which puzzles me is that a code below works just fine:

p<-ggplot(Data,aes(x=DATE,y=PRINCIPAL))
p+geom_point()

So I am missing something when trying to create a bar chart..

Br,
Jack

messages.subject: Re: How to remove duplicated legends
messages.body_plain:
hi. Josh's explanation will help to understand legends.
here is another workaround, without hacking ScaleSizeContinuous.

a)

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y))+

  stat_sum(aes(fill = ..prop.., group = x), geom = 'tile')+
  scale_fill_gradient('Percent', low='white', high='steelblue',
formatter = 'percent')+

  scale_size(legend=FALSE)

b)

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y))+
  stat_sum(aes(size = NULL, fill = ..prop.., group = x), geom = 'tile')+

  scale_fill_gradient('Percent', low='white', high='steelblue',
formatter = 'percent')

probably b) is more efficient.

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

Hi Kim,
Here is one way:

## ADD LABELS
## First compute statistics. Note that this is just an example, and
probably not the way you should actually do it.

mstats <- ddply(ds_test, .(individual), function(DF) {
  m <- lm(size ~ time, data=DF)
  coefs <- coef(summary(m))
  R <- data.frame(estimate = coefs["time", "Estimate"], p =
coefs["time", "Pr(>|t|)"])
  R$label <- with(R, paste("b = ", format(estimate,digits=2), ", ", "p
= ", format(p, digits=2), sep=""))

  return(R)
}
                )

mstats$time <- (diff(range(ds_test$time))/2)
mstats$size <- (max(ds_test$size) + 1)

## Add the labels to the plot
p <- qplot(time,size,data=ds_test,geom=c("point", "smooth"),method="lm" ) +
facet_wrap(~individual)
p + geom_text(aes(label=label), data=mstats, size=4

HTH,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I'm going to chime in here only because I spent a half hour working on it :)

I used somewhat different functions from Ista, but we seem to have looked at the problem the same way.

I'm using a little trick that Hadley showed a while back about using dlply() in the plyr package to run a sequence of models and then cherry picking output from the resulting list of model objects.

library(ggplot2)   # will load plyr automatically

# Generate the models
mods <- dlply(ds_test, .(individual), function(x) lm(size ~ time, data = x))

# Functions to extract the slope and p-value from a generic lm model object x
slope <- function(x) coef(x)[2]
pval <- function(x) anova(x)$`Pr(>F)`[1]

# Apply the two functions to the list of models - both yield two column
# data frames with individual as one of the variables. This is convenient
# when we join the two data frames.
s1 <- ldply(mods, slope)
s2 <- ldply(mods, pval)
ds_out <- join(s1, s2)

# Rename the third column:
names(ds_out)[3] <- 'pvalue'
# Add two columns of strings to use in the faceted plots
ds_out$slab <- sprintf('Slope: %7.5f', ds_out$time)
ds_out$plab <- sprintf('p-value: %7.5f', ds_out$pvalue)

# Fire up ggplot():
ggplot(ds_test, aes(x = time, y = size) ) +
     geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = 'lm') +
     facet_wrap(~ individual) +
     geom_text(data = ds_out, aes(x = 0, y = -5, lab = plab), size = 3, hjust = 0) +
     geom_text(data = ds_out, aes(x = 0, y = -2.5, lab = slab), size = 3, hjust = 0)

Other than a couple of little details, the result is essentially the same as Ista's.

Thanks for bringing this problem up - it was a good excuse to practice running multiple models at once :)

HTH,
Dennis

> library(ggplot2)   # will load plyr automatically
>
> # Generate the models
> mods <- dlply(ds_test, .(individual), function(x) lm(size ~ time, data = x))
>
> # Functions to extract the slope and p-value from a generic lm model object x
> slope <- function(x) coef(x)[2]
> pval <- function(x) anova(x)$`Pr(>F)`[1]
>
> # Apply the two functions to the list of models - both yield two column
> # data frames with individual as one of the variables. This is convenient
> # when we join the two data frames.
> s1 <- ldply(mods, slope)
> s2 <- ldply(mods, pval)
> ds_out <- join(s1, s2)
>
> # Rename the third column:
> names(ds_out)[3] <- 'pvalue'
> # Add two columns of strings to use in the faceted plots
> ds_out$slab <- sprintf('Slope: %7.5f', ds_out$time)
> ds_out$plab <- sprintf('p-value: %7.5f', ds_out$pvalue)
>
> # Fire up ggplot():
> ggplot(ds_test, aes(x = time, y = size) ) +
>      geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = 'lm') +
>      facet_wrap(~ individual) +
>      geom_text(data = ds_out, aes(x = 0, y = -5, lab = plab), size = 3, hjust = 0) +
>      geom_text(data = ds_out, aes(x = 0, y = -2.5, lab = slab), size = 3, hjust = 0)
>
> Other than a couple of little details, the result is essentially the same as Ista's.
>

>
> HTH,
> Dennis

messages.subject: Re: unexpected grouping behavior
messages.body_plain:
Well

1) You only have two levels in your grouping factor, so that is all
you will get, but
2) It does create 4 lines, two are distinguished by shape, two by
colour, which is exactly what you asked for (though perhaps not what
you want).

I get the feeling you are angling for:

ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y, group=interaction(factor(origin), factor(sample)))) +
  geom_path()

which as the grouping variable passes the interaction of origin and
sample.  You are free to colour as you please.

HTH,

Josh

ian,

The reason for the difference is that, by default, group is set to the
interaction of all the other aesthetic factors.  So in your second
example, there is an implicit
group=interaction(factor(origin),factor(sample)) since one is used for
color and one for linetype.  In the first example, you override the
default group specification (factor(origin)) with a different one
(factor(sample)).

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

a rectengular mesh of grid points: say 87 latitudes and 61 longitudes.

Examine the height distributions at individual longitudes and pooling
over latitudes.
In my real world data set, longitude translates to time, latitude is a
sample-ID and height is a concentration.

For each longitude separately, rank the heights and divide the ranks
by the number of latitude values (87) to obtain approximate quantiles
q.
Plot contours of equal q in the (longitude, height)-plane using
geom_contour.

require(ggplot2)

Ranks             <- apply(volcano,2,rank,ties.method='random')
#  ie ranking is done for each value of the 2nd index (longitude)
separately.

colnames(profiles)<- c("longitude","height",'q')
profiles.df       <- data.frame(profiles)
Graph<-ggplot(profiles.df,aes(x=longitude,y=height,z=q))+
stat_contour(linetype=1,size =
0.25,colour="grey50",breaks=seq(from=0.25,by=0.25,to=0.75))

Hi all,

This strays a bit from strictly ggplot2, but I thought that it was applicable enough to ask here anyways (besides as one of my teachers liked to say, "There's no award for being timid").

My basic question is: how does one create the "best" or ideal graph to communicate a particular set of data or results in ggplot2?  Assuming there is no simple answer (a la the answer to the universe, 42), what is a good way to go about learning?  I find that most books on statistics have a dearth, if any, advice on graphical presentations.  I looked for books that seemed to deal in general with graphics and collected this list from the references in the ggplot2 and lattice books and a paper by Cleveland.

Does anyone have additional references they think are good, or have a particular recommendation for a neophyte?  Would a list of recommended reading be appropriate for the wiki?

------------------------------------------------------------------

***William Cleveland. Visualizing Data. Hobart Press, Summit, New Jersey, 1993.

***William Cleveland. The Elements of Graphing Data. Wadsworth, Monterey, California, 1985.

***John Tukey. Exploratory Data Analysis. Addison-Wesley Publishing Co., Reading, Massachusetts, 1977.

**Paul Murrell. R Graphics. Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2005.

**John Chambers, William Cleveland, Beat Kleiner, and Paul Tukey. Graphical methods for Data Analysis. Wadsworth, 1983.

**Leland Wilkinson. The Grammar of Graphics. Springer, New York, 1999.

**Edward R. Tufte. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Graphics Press, 2001.

Edward R. Tufte. Envisioning Information. Graphics Press, 1990.

Edward R. Tufte. Visual Explanations. Graphics Press, 1997.

Edward R. Tufte. Beautiful Evidence. Graphics Press, 2006.

Paul Murrell. Investigations in Graphical Statistics. PhD thesis, The University of Auckland, 1998.

M. Friendly. Visualizing Categorical Data. SAS Institute, Carey, NC, 2000. ISBN 1-58

W. C. Brinton. Graphical Methods for Presenting Facts. Engineering Magazine Co., NewYork, 1914.

C. F. Schmid and S. E. Schmid. Handbook of Graphic Presentation. Wiley,New York, 1979.

I. Spence and S. Lewandowsky. Graphical perception. In J. Fox and Long S., editors, Modern Methods of Data Analysis, Beverly Hills, CA, to appear. Sage Publications.

H. Wainer and D. Thissen. Graphical data analysis. Ann. Rev. Psychol.,, 32:191–241, 1981.

William Cleveland. A model for studying display methods of statistical graphics. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 2:323–364, 1993b. URL http://stat.bell-labs.com/doc/93.4.ps.

William Cleveland, editor. The Collected Works of John W. Tukey, Volume V: Graphics 1965–1985. Wadsworth & Brooks/Cole Advanced Books & Software, Monterey, CA, 1988.

------------------------------------------------------------------

Asterisks indicate how many times I saw a particular references in the three sources I drew on.

Thanks and tongue lashings for irrelevance willingly accepted,

Josh

P.S.  I saw a new type of chart in Excel today.  It takes the idea of a bar chart, but makes it 3d.  If you're still not content, you can choose tapered cones instead of rectangles/cubes.  These may also be stacked for a truly confusing experience.

--
Joshua Wiley
Ph.D. Student, Health Psychology
University of California, Los Angeles
http://www.joshuawiley.com/

So, I suspect it isn't working because contour is wanting a complete grid...?

Seems like you want lines joining quantiles of height within longitude

  data.frame(q = probs, height = quantile(df$height, probs = probs))})

qplot(longitude, height, data = quants, geom = "line", colour = factor(q))

Charlotte

> >>>
> >>> Hi,
> >>>
> >>> ggplot2 tries to present as concise of legends as possible, however, when
> >>> information is unique, there must be unique legends.  Two scales are
> >>> involved here, scale_fill_gradient() and scale_size().  When the title of
> >>> scale_fill_gradient() is changed, the title must also be changed on
> >>> scale_size() in order for the legends to be collapsed.  There is a second
> >>> issue, the formatting of the scale_fill_gradient() legend was changed, so it
> >>> must also be changed on scale_size() in order for them to be collapsed.
> >>>  However, scale_size() lacks a formatter argument.  Here is what the code
> >>> would need to look like:
> >>>
> >>> ggplot(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
> >>>  stat_sum(aes(fill = ..prop.., group = x), geom = 'tile') +
> >>>  scale_fill_gradient('Percent', low='white', high='steelblue', formatter =
> >>> 'percent') +
> >>>  scale_size('Percent', formatter = 'percent')
> >>>
> >>> and here is a patch to scale_size() to make the above code actually work.
> >>>
> >>> Cheers,
> >>>
> >>> Josh
> >>>
> >>> @Hadley, all I did was add a formatter = identity argument to the function
> >>> and formatter = formatter to the super$new call.
> >>>
> >>>
> >>> ScaleSizeContinuous <- proto(ScaleContinuous, expr={
> >>>   doc <- TRUE
> >>>   common <- NULL
> >>>   .input <- .output <- "size"
> >>>   aliases <- c("scale_area", "scale_size")
> >>>
> >>>   new <- function(., name=NULL, limits=NULL, breaks=NULL, labels=NULL,
> >>> formatter = identity, trans = NULL, to = c(1, 6), legend = TRUE) {
> >>>
> >>>     b_and_l <- check_breaks_and_labels(breaks, labels)
> >>>
> >>>     .super$new(., name=name, limits=limits, breaks=b_and_l$breaks,
> >>> labels=b_and_l$labels, formatter = formatter, trans=trans, variable =
> >>> "size", to = to, legend = legend)
> >>>   }
> >>>
> >>>   map <- function(., values) {
> >>>     rescale(values, .$to, .$input_set())
> >>>   }
> >>>   output_breaks <- function(.) .$map(.$input_breaks())
> >>>
> >>>   objname <- "size_continuous"
> >>>   desc <- "Size scale for continuous variable"
> >>>   seealso <- list(
> >>>     "scale_manual" = "for sizing discrete variables"
> >>>   )
> >>>   desc_params <- list(
> >>>     "to" = "a numeric vector of length 2 that specifies the minimum and
> >>> maximum size of the plotting symbol after transformation."
> >>>   )
> >>>
> >>>   icon <- function(.) {
> >>>     pos <- c(0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75)
> >>>     circleGrob(pos, pos, r=(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4)/2.5),
> >>> gp=gpar(fill="grey50", col=NA))
> >>>   }
> >>>
> >>>   examples <- function(.) {
> >>>     (p <- qplot(mpg, cyl, data=mtcars, size=cyl))
> >>>     p + scale_size("cylinders")
> >>>     p + scale_size("number\nof\ncylinders")
> >>>
> >>>     p + scale_size(to = c(0, 10))
> >>>     p + scale_size(to = c(1, 2))
> >>>
> >>>     # Map area, instead of width/radius
> >>>     # Perceptually, this is a little better
> >>>     p + scale_area()
> >>>     p + scale_area(to = c(1, 25))
> >>>
> >>>     # Also works with factors, but not a terribly good
> >>>     # idea, unless your factor is ordered, as in this example
> >>>     qplot(mpg, cyl, data=mtcars, size=factor(cyl))
> >>>
> >>>     # To control the size mapping for discrete variable, use
> >>>     # scale_size_manual:
> >>>     last_plot() + scale_size_manual(values=c(2,4,6))
> >>>
> >>>   }
> >>>
> >>> })

messages.subject: line plot with overlay
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I want to overlay the average of a given dataset onto a simple line
plot of the same dataset.

Here is a simple example:

#generate some data
estimation <- sample(1:100,8)
#add information on trial
trial <- rep(1:4,2)
#add information on participant
subject<- rep(1:2, each = 4)

#put it together into a data frame
data<-data.frame(estimation,subject,trial)

#plot the estimations in a line plot
g <- ggplot(data, aes(x=trial, y=estimation, group=subject)) +
geom_line()

#up to this point everything is fine as as expected
#now I want to add an overlay line in read displaying the means of
estimation for each trial

g + geom_line(stat="summary", fun.y = "mean", colour = "red")

#the result is that the two lines turn red (instead of staying black)
and the line with the average is missing (I would like to end up with
three lines)

Any advice??

Thanks a lot
Michael

messages.subject: Translating from qplot to ggplot
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to visualize the results of a strategic game using R and ggplot2 (overkill but a good training ground for a novice, I thought).

The data are here:

> result1 <- read.csv( "ftp://godesberg.homelinux.net/result1.csv" )
> result1 <- result1[-1]
> teams <- unique( result1$Tm )

I get what I want (ugly, I know, just interim stage[1]) with

> library( ggplot2 )
> qplot( rnd, Equity, data = result1, fill = Tm, group = Tm )
  + geom_bar( stat = "identity", position = "dodge" )
  + scale_fill_hue( "Team Name", breaks = teams, labels = teams )
  + xlab("Game Round")

but I've spent hours now, using the online documentation and Hadley's book, trying to translate that into a set of ggplot commands / layers -- without success. I get bits and peices translated but not exactly what I have with the qplot command.

Would be extremely grateful for a pointer in the right direction!

Thanks,
Rainer

[1] Using lines instead of bars, and other columns instead of Equity, I get already quite far

messages.subject: Re: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot
messages.subject_clean: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,
  without a reproducible example I don't know what was wrong about
your legend.
If it helps, the way to collapse multiple legend sections that map the
same variable to different scales is to make the name and labels match
up between scales.
I assume that you want to specify the shapes that you are using -
otherwise change to scale_shape_discrete and remove the values call:

library(ggplot2)

fakedata <- data.frame(RW = 1:5, EWW = 0:4, LWW = 4.5:0.5)

cols <- c("LWW" = "red", "EWW" = "black")

dat <- melt(fakedata, measure.vars = c("EWW", "LWW"))

qplot(RW, value, xlab = "Ring width (mm)", ylab = "Earlywood or
latewood width (mm)", data = dat, colour = variable, shape = variable)
+
	scale_colour_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = cols, breaks =
c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood")) +
	scale_shape_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = c(2, 5), breaks =
c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood"))

-Allan

Ranier,

I wouldn't suspect that 2.11.1 would be a problem. Usually when it's a problem is when someone says they're having problems on R 2.6 or something ridiculously out of date. My other machine is X86_64 and things usually run fine.

I might have figured it out just now.

> > Error in +geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") :
> >  invalid argument to unary operator

When you have another line make sure that the + goes at the end of the line and not at the beginning of the line.

Example:

ggplotobject +
xlab('X axis label')

NOT

ggplotobject
+xlab ('X axis label')

Does it work then?

Brandon

messages.subject_clean: fill in legend of black & white crossbar plot
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have prepared a coloured graph (attached) for publication in a journal which I now have to change into black and white :-( (attached). Otherwise, I’d have to pay ca. 1000 $ for 3 graphs, seriously.

I have attached a reproducible R script. It first presents the graph in colour and then in black and white which shows the dilemma.

Ideally, I would like to have the “line” AND the “fill” in the legend, not only the “line”. “Fill” only would be good too. Of course I could use different line types but for a crossbar it would look a bit stupid. The other alternative would be to use a white line for the second group but really, that would not produce a great legend as well.

If anybody could help me include the fill in the legend or has a good alternative I would be very grateful.

Best wishes,

Martin

messages.subject: RE: fill in legend of black & white crossbar plot
messages.subject_clean: fill in legend of black & white crossbar plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

As a workaround, you can just add a layer which takes fill as a valid aesthetic (I guess, after looking at the online documentation, that’s the reason why if you only include geom_crossbar the fill doesn’t appear in the legend [e.g. hollow bar …]); in the code bellow I just added geom_smooth() (you only receive a warning saying you have only one x value and nothing to draw).

Hope this helps, and congratulations,

fernando

ggplot(df, aes(fill = group, colour = group, y = resp, x = trt)) +

                geom_crossbar(limits,  width = 0.7, position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), size = 0.8) +

                geom_smooth() +

                scale_fill_manual(values = alpha(c("white", "black"), 0.3), name = "") +

                scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "black"), name = "") +

                scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(36, 50, 2), name = "") +

                scale_x_discrete(name = "") +

                opts(legend.position = c(0.764, 0.833),

                               legend.background = theme_rect(colour = 0),

                               legend.text = theme_text(face = "italic", size = 20),

                               legend.title = theme_blank()) +

                opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 20, vjust = 1),

                               axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 20, hjust = 1)) +

                opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 27, hjust = 0.561, vjust = 0.3),

                               axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 27, angle = 90, vjust = 0.685, hjust = 0.78)) +

                opts(plot.margin = unit (c(1.1, 1, 1.28, 1.23), "lines"))

messages.subject: Re: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot
messages.subject_clean: Changing plot symbols in multivariate scatterplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Thanks for the reproducible example. There are some ways to make the plot more efficient, though.

I find it very useful to define the legend labels as levels of a factor in the data and assign the name I want for the legend to be its variable name in the data - all I'm really doing is relabeling the factor variable and giving it an evocative name.

dat$WoodType <- factor(dat$variable, labels = c('Earlywood', 'Latewood'))

This makes the call a lot easier, removing the need for the color scale entirely and making the scale_shape_manual call straightforward:

qplot(RW, value, xlab = "Ring width (mm)",
       ylab = "Earlywood or latewood width (mm)", data = dat,

       colour = WoodType, shape = WoodType) +
   scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 18))

I wanted to make the point size bigger, so since I use ggplot() instead, it was just easier for me to write it that way:

ggplot(dat, aes(x = RW, y = value, colour = WoodType, shape = WoodType)) +
      geom_point(size = 3) + scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 18)) +
      xlab("Ring width (mm)") +
      ylab("Earlywood or latewood width (mm)")

BTW, I got an error when I tried running your code:

> qplot(RW, value, xlab = "Ring width (mm)", ylab = "Earlywood or

+ latewood width (mm)", data = dat, colour = variable, shape = variable)

> +
+        scale_colour_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = cols, breaks =

+ c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood")) +

+        scale_shape_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = c(2, 5), breaks =

+ c("EWW", "LWW"), labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood"))
Error in +scale_colour_manual(name = "Wood Type", values = cols, breaks = c("EWW",  :
  invalid argument to unary operator

I think the problem is that your cols object contained both breaks and values and you used all three (including labels) in the scale_colour_manual() call. Coordinating breaks, values and labels takes some practice, which is why it's easier to simplify the plot call as much as possible by carefully arranging the data in advance.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dennis,
  your code is more succinct and I also prefer ggplot(). Thanks!

I was just trying to show how to collapse legends on similar scales.
The code I wrote works if Google hadn't broken my first + sign to its
own line.
The lesson for me is to keep line lengths below 75 characters.
Here it is again with shorter line lengths:

fakedata <- data.frame(RW = 1:5, EWW = 0:4, LWW = 4.5:0.5)
cols <- c("LWW" = "red", "EWW" = "black")
dat <- melt(fakedata, measure.vars = c("EWW", "LWW"))

qplot(RW, value, xlab = "Ring width (mm)",
	ylab = "Earlywood or latewood width (mm)",
	data = dat, colour = variable, shape = variable) +
	scale_colour_manual(name = "Wood Type",
		values = cols, breaks = c("EWW", "LWW"),
		labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood")) +
	scale_shape_manual(name = "Wood Type",
		values = c(2, 5), breaks = c("EWW", "LWW"),
		labels = c("Earlywood", "Latewood"))

messages.body_plain:
Hi ggplot2,

I'm trying to add a scalebar to an existing ggplot. I already have the
appropriate polygonGrob, I only can;t get it to plot correctly. An
example:

library(sp) # may need to install this one
library(ggplot2)

data(meuse.grid)

grid.newpage()
ggplot(aes(x  = x, y = y, fill = dist), data = meuse.grid) +
geom_tile()
grid.add("panel", polygonGrob(), grep = TRUE)

I now have plotted a simple polygon over the existing plot. The
challenge now is to plot a polygon that has the coordinates system of
the panel and not in npc coordinates:

p1 = polygonGrob(x = c(181e3, 181e3, 181.5e3, 181.5e3),
            y = c(330e3, 331e3, 331e3, 330e3))
grid.newpage()
ggplot(aes(x  = x, y = y, fill = dist), data = meuse.grid) +
geom_tile()
grid.add("panel", p1, grep = TRUE)

The problem is that the coordinates in p1 are not in npc. When I try
to convert:

p2 = polygonGrob(x = convertUnit(unit(c(181e3, 181e3, 181.5e3,
181.5e3), "native"), "npc"),
            y = convertUnit(unit(c(330e3, 331e3, 331e3, 330e3),
"native"), "npc"))
grid.newpage()

messages.subject_clean: AW: fill in legend of black & white crossbar plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fernando,

Thanks for this excellent solution! I will probably need it for many future graphs. Thanks also for reorganising my code. It is now much clearer. When checking your code I realised that some of my code was actually unnecessary. The code now reads:

ggplot(df, aes(fill = group, colour = group, y = resp, x = trt)) +
    geom_crossbar(limits,  width = 0.7, position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), size = 0.8) +

    geom_smooth(size = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = alpha(c("white", "black"), 0.4), name = "") +

    scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "black"), name = "") +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(36, 50, 2), name = "") +
    scale_x_discrete(name = "") +

    opts(legend.position = c(0.764, 0.8334),

        legend.background = theme_rect(colour = 0),

        legend.key = theme_rect(colour = 1, size = 0.6),

        legend.text = theme_text(face = "italic", size = 20),
        legend.title = theme_blank()) +
    opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 20, vjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 20, hjust = 1)) +

    opts(plot.margin = unit (c(1.1, 1, 2, 2), "lines"))

    grid.text("cell type of eggs", x = unit(0.56, "npc"), y = unit(0.05, "npc"), gp=gpar(fontsize = 27))
    grid.text("time to be replaced [h]", x = unit(0.04, "npc"), y = unit(0.552, "npc"), rot = 90, gp=gpar(fontsize = 27))

I have also attached the graph as a PDF.

Do you know if this feature will eventually be included in geom_crossbar? I cannot see a logical reason why "fill" should not be included in the legend of geom_crossbar.

Best wishes,

Martin

Betreff: RE: fill in legend of black & white crossbar plot

Hi Martin,

As a workaround, you can just add a layer which takes fill as a valid aesthetic (I guess, after looking at the online documentation, that’s the reason why if you only include geom_crossbar the fill doesn’t appear in the legend [e.g. hollow bar …]); in the code bellow I just added geom_smooth() (you only receive a warning saying you have only one x value and nothing to draw).

Hope this helps, and congratulations,

fernando

ggplot(df, aes(fill = group, colour = group, y = resp, x = trt)) +

                geom_crossbar(limits,  width = 0.7, position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), size = 0.8) +

                geom_smooth() +

                scale_fill_manual(values = alpha(c("white", "black"), 0.3), name = "") +

                scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "black"), name = "") +

                scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(36, 50, 2), name = "") +

                scale_x_discrete(name = "") +

                opts(legend.position = c(0.764, 0.833),

                               legend.background = theme_rect(colour = 0),

                               legend.text = theme_text(face = "italic", size = 20),

                               legend.title = theme_blank()) +

                opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 20, vjust = 1),

                               axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 20, hjust = 1)) +

                opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 27, hjust = 0.561, vjust = 0.3),

                               axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 27, angle = 90, vjust = 0.685, hjust = 0.78)) +

                opts(plot.margin = unit (c(1.1, 1, 1.28, 1.23), "lines"))

Dear all,

I have prepared a coloured graph (attached) for publication in a journal which I now have to change into black and white :-( (attached). Otherwise, I’d have to pay ca. 1000 $ for 3 graphs, seriously.

I have attached a reproducible R script. It first presents the graph in colour and then in black and white which shows the dilemma.

Ideally, I would like to have the “line” AND the “fill” in the legend, not only the “line”. “Fill” only would be good too. Of course I could use different line types but for a crossbar it would look a bit stupid. The other alternative would be to use a white line for the second group but really, that would not produce a great legend as well.

If anybody could help me include the fill in the legend or has a good alternative I would be very grateful.

messages.subject: Re: Bar chart without vertical grid
messages.body_plain:
Sorry, I did misunderstand.  I thought you wanted to remove only the minor vertical gridlines, but you want to remove all of them (kind of a keynote style bar chart).  Ideal here would be a panel.grid.major.y and panel.grid.minor.y param to opts but AFAIK those don't exist.

I messed around trying to do it with geom_hline etc, but this works better:

data  <- data.frame(Name = c("A","B","C","D","E","F","G","H"), y = c(100,200,300,400,200,300,400,350))

ggplot(data,aes(x=Name,y=y)) + geom_bar()

grid.remove("panel.grid.minor.x.polyline",grep=T)
grid.remove("panel.grid.major.x.polyline",grep=T)
grid.remove("panel.grid.minor.y.polyline",grep=T)

Note that ggsave seems to discard these edits, so I had to wrap this in png() and dev.off().

Anyone know why ggsave() ignores grid level edits?

I used the instructions here:

https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Editing-raw-grid-objects-from-a-ggplot

Thx,
James

hi, try this:

guide_grid <- function(theme, x.minor, x.major, y.minor, y.major) {
  ggname("grill", grobTree(
    theme_render(theme, "panel.background"),

    theme_render(
      theme, "panel.grid.minor", name = "y",
      x = rep(0:1, length(y.minor)), y = rep(y.minor, each=2),
      id.lengths = rep(2, length(y.minor))
    ),
      theme_render(
      theme, "panel.grid.major", name = "y",
      x = rep(0:1, length(y.major)), y = rep(y.major, each=2),
      id.lengths = rep(2, length(y.major))
    )
  ))
}
assignInNamespace("guide_grid", guide_grid, pos="package:ggplot2")

@Mark, this was exactly the problem I was facing.

The problem is that if I want to use scale_fill_* to change the color of the polygon (alternating black and white) that could conflict with other geoms (e.g. geom_tile) that already defined the fill. I could add a separate geom_polygon for each subpolygon of the scalebar (e.g. 5), but do you have a better suggestion to circumvent the problem of defining scale_fill_* twice?

Paul

messages.subject: viewport grid layout
messages.body_plain:
I am using ggplot2's grid layout in viewport to plot multiple residual
and predicted-vs-observed plots on one page.  I am trying to gain
space for the plots by removing axis labels and tick labels by setting
them to NULL or "", but have not been able to get the plot area to
expand into the space formerly occupied by labels.  Any suggestions?
Code below.

## Observed vs. predicted
## Plot six to a page
dev.new <http://dev.new>()
theme_set(theme_bw());
theme_update(theme_text(size = 11, vjust = 0.0, colour = "black"));
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(3, 2)))
print(O1 + geom_line(aes(x=TSS_obs, y=TSS_obs)) + geom_text(aes(x=0.5,
y=3.8), label="a) TSS", size = 4), vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1,
layout.pos.col = 1) )
print(O2 + geom_line(aes(x=TOC_obs, y=TOC_obs)) + geom_text(aes(x=2.7,
y=3.9), label="b) TOC", size = 4), vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1,
layout.pos.col = 2) )
print(O3 + geom_line(aes(x=DOC_obs, y=DOC_obs)) + geom_text(aes(x=2.7,
y=3.9), label="c) DOC", size = 4), vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 2,
layout.pos.col = 1) )
print(O4 + geom_line(aes(x=TN_obs, y=TN_obs)) + geom_text(aes(x=0.46,
y=0.95), label="d) TN", size = 4), vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 2,
layout.pos.col = 2) )
print(O5 + geom_line(aes(x=DON_obs, y=DON_obs)) + geom_text(aes(x=0.3,
y=0.93), label="f) DON", size = 4), vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 3,
layout.pos.col = 1) )
print(O6 + geom_line(aes(x=DON_obs, y=NH4_obs)) + geom_text(aes(x=0.3,
y=0.93), label="f) DON", size = 4), vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 3,
layout.pos.col = 1) )

messages.subject: Re: Adding a scalebar to an existing ggplot
messages.subject_clean: Adding a scalebar to an existing ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If the scalebar is black and white, you should only need two calls to
geom_rect (or rather geom_path i guess). Something like this perhaps,

library(ggplot2)

p = qplot(1:10,1:10)
## p

makeScaleBar <- function(x=8,y=2,width=2,N=4, ...){

  dlong = data.frame(x=x - width/2,
    xend = x + width/2,
    y=y, yend=y)

  dshort = data.frame(x=x - width/2 + seq(0, N-1,by=2)*width/N,
    xend = x - width/2 + (1 + seq(0, N-1,by=2))*width/N,
    y=y, yend=y)

  list(geom_segment(data=dlong, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend),
colour="black", ...),
       geom_segment(data=dshort, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend),
colour="white", ...))

}

p + makeScaleBar(N=5, size=5)

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: viewport grid layout
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You can play with the theme settings using opts(),

library(ggplot2)

p = qplot(1:10,1:10)

snug.opts <- opts(axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
             axis.title.x = theme_blank(),
             axis.title.y = theme_blank(),
             axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "lines"),
             axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "lines"),
             panel.margin = unit(0, "lines"),
             plot.margin = unit(c(-0.5,0,0,-0.5), "lines"))

fourplots <- replicate(4, p + snug.opts, simplify=FALSE)

library(gridExtra)

do.call(grid.arrange, fourplots)

HTH,

baptiste

of contributed code section for ggplot?

Paul

to the scaled real-world coordinates of the map and in arbitrary
scalebar units (ideally).  Think in terms of a map of Italy with a scale
showing the measure of a kilometer or 100km.

The scalebar and the map should not interfere with each other (the
scalebar colors should not show up on a legend, for example). The
scalebar should also rescale if the data are zoomed (changed
presentation or data limits) and ideally change position and number of
scalebar segments.

The geom_polygon seems like it is a likely existing geom to start with.
It would have to be constructed according to the coordinates of the data
and the limits of the presentation.  The polygon segments would be
adjusted according to the units of measure.  The scalebar segments would
alternate color.  The scalebar segments would not show up in the
legend.  The scalebar would be anchored in space according to a
positioning specification, with a possible default given the extents of
the data on the map.

It seems that multiple viewports might separate the scalebar from the
map and get rid of conflicts.  This has two problems: 1. not everyone
wants to deal with a plot with multiple viewports. 2.  It may not be
possible to scale the scalebar viewport so that it has the scalebar at
the right proportions.

There seems to be a significant impedance mismatch with the notion of a
scalebar mixed with a gplot map.  Maybe someone has some ideas, though.
It would be a worthwhile thing to accomplish.

I wonder if a graticule might be a more feasible option?

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A preliminary version of the addScaleBar() function is given below, with an example using a dataset from the sp-package. Any comments are appreciated.

Paul

makeNiceNumber = function(num, num.pretty = 1) {
  # Rounding provided by code from Maarten Plieger
  return((round(num/10^(round(log10(num))-1))*(10^(round(log10(num))-1))))
}

createBoxPolygon = function(llcorner, width, height) {
  relativeCoords = data.frame(c(0, 0, width, width, 0), c(0, height, height, 0, 0))
  names(relativeCoords) = names(llcorner)
  return(t(apply(relativeCoords, 1, function(x) llcorner + x)))
}

addScaleBar = function(ggplot_obj, spatial_obj, attribute, addParams = list()) {
  addParamsDefaults = list(noBins = 5, xname = "x", yname = "y", unit = "m", placement = "bottomright",
                           sbLengthPct = 0.3, sbHeightvsWidth = 1/14)
  addParams = modifyList(addParamsDefaults, addParams)

  range_x = max(spatial_obj[[addParams[["xname"]]]]) - min(spatial_obj[[addParams[["xname"]]]])
  range_y = max(spatial_obj[[addParams[["yname"]]]]) - min(spatial_obj[[addParams[["yname"]]]])
  lengthScalebar = addParams[["sbLengthPct"]] * range_x
  widthBin = makeNiceNumber(lengthScalebar / addParams[["noBins"]])
  heightBin = lengthScalebar * addParams[["sbHeightvsWidth"]]
  lowerLeftCornerScaleBar = c(x = max(spatial_obj[[addParams[["xname"]]]]) - (widthBin * addParams[["noBins"]]),
                              y = min(spatial_obj[[addParams[["yname"]]]]))

  scaleBarPolygon = do.call("rbind", lapply(0:(addParams[["noBins"]] - 1), function(n) {
    dum = data.frame(createBoxPolygon(lowerLeftCornerScaleBar + c((n * widthBin), 0), widthBin, heightBin))
    if(!(n + 1) %% 2 == 0) dum$cat = "odd" else dum$cat = "even"
    return(dum)
  }))
  scaleBarPolygon[[attribute]] = min(spatial_obj[[attribute]])
  textScaleBar = data.frame(x = lowerLeftCornerScaleBar[[addParams[["xname"]]]] + (c(0:(addParams[["noBins"]])) * widthBin),
                            y = lowerLeftCornerScaleBar[[addParams[["yname"]]]],
                            label = as.character(0:(addParams[["noBins"]]) * widthBin))
  textScaleBar[[attribute]] = min(spatial_obj[[attribute]])

  return(ggplot_obj +
    geom_polygon(data = subset(scaleBarPolygon, cat == "odd"), fill = "black", color = "black", legend = FALSE) +
    geom_polygon(data = subset(scaleBarPolygon, cat == "even"), fill = "white", color = "black", legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), color = "black", size = 6, data = textScaleBar, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1.2, legend = FALSE))
}

data(meuse)
data(meuse.grid)
ggobj = ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = zinc), data = meuse) + geom_point()
addScaleBar(ggobj, meuse, "zinc", addParams = list(noBins = 5))

Hi Vikas,
I think the usual way to do it is to set the colour of the text the
same way you set the colour of the lines (i.e., as an aesthetic
mapping). The advantage of this approach is that if you change the
colour scale (e.g., with scale_colour_hue() your changes will be
consistent across all geoms using that scale.

Best,
Ista

> >   heightBin = lengthScalebar * addParams[["sbHeightvsWidth"]]
> >   lowerLeftCornerScaleBar = c(x = max(spatial_obj[[addParams[["xname"]]]]) - (widthBin * addParams[["noBins"]]),
> >                               y = min(spatial_obj[[addParams[["yname"]]]]))

messages.subject: Re: how to use spline() with ggplot?
messages.subject_clean: how to use spline() with ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's an example:

x = seq(0, 2 * pi, length = 500)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = sin(x) + rnorm(500, s = 0.3))

library(splines)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
     stat_smooth(data = g, aes(x = x, y = y), method = 'lm',
                          formula = y ~ ns(x, 3), col = 'red', size = 2, se= FALSE)

It should be simpler if you use lm() with one of the spline functions generating the basis matrix. I used ns() here, but one could use other basis functions equally well. Here's a different example using the rcs() function in package rms:

library(rms)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() +
     stat_smooth(data = g, aes(x = x, y = y), method = 'lm',
                          formula = y ~ rcs(x, 4), col = 'red', size = 2, se= FALSE)

The graph should be essentially the same. The se argument is unneeded because confidence curves won't be plotted if you specify se = TRUE.

HTH,
Dennis

You could use the function in scale_hue that selects the colors. A
standalone version is in the new scales package,

https://github.com/hadley/scales/raw/master/R/pal-hue.r

(for some reason I can't source() this url so I copy it here)

hue_pal <- function(h = c(0, 360) + 15, c = 100, l = 65, h.start = 0,
direction = 1) {

  function(n) {
    if ((diff(h) %% 360) < 1) {
      h[2] <- h[2] - 360 / n
    }

    rotate <- function(x) (x + h.start) %% 360 * direction
    hues <- rotate(seq(h[1], h[2], length = n))

    hcl(hues, c, l)
  }
}

messages.subject: Re: geom_line displaying blank grid
messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much!  What a simple solution.

On Nov 29, 9:26 pm, Dennis Murphy <djmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> Ancient ggplot2 secret:
>
> stuff=data.frame(time = factor(time),means)
> ggplot()+geom_line(data=stuff,aes(time,means, group = 1))
>
> The group = 1 snippet is the magic code you need to plot a line between
> numeric y's when the x-values are factor levels.
>
> HTH,
> Dennis
>

> On Mon, Nov 29, 2010 at 2:19 PM, Jahan <jahan.mohiud...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,

> > means=c(0.638,0.786,1.292,0.220,0.450,0.570,0.438)
> > stuff=data.frame(time,means)
> > ggplot()+geom_line(data=stuff,aes(time,means))
>
> > Hopefully you will see the problem I am having.  I suspect it might
